result.summary: The gods quarrel over Troy, and Jove agrees to let Minerva make the Trojans break the truce. Minerva persuades Pandarus to wound Menelaus, Machaon treats him, and Agamemnon rallies and rebukes his captains. The armies clash and many die on both sides.

scenes.title: Council of the gods
scenes.summary: Jove teases Juno about Troy's fate. They bargain, and Minerva is sent down to make the Trojans break their oaths.
scenes.stakes: Troy's survival and Juno's hard-won effort against Priam's city.

scenes.title: Pandarus wounds Menelaus
scenes.summary: Minerva, disguised as Laodocus, persuades Pandarus to shoot Menelaus. The arrow is turned by Minerva and only grazes him.
scenes.stakes: Menelaus's life, and the truce sworn between the armies.

scenes.title: Machaon heals Menelaus
scenes.summary: Agamemnon laments and vows vengeance. Talthybius fetches Machaon, who treats the wound as the Trojans advance.
scenes.stakes: Menelaus's life and the Achaean expedition.

scenes.title: Agamemnon reviews his captains
scenes.summary: Agamemnon goes among his leaders, praising Idomeneus, the Ajaxes and Nestor, and rebuking Menestheus and Ulysses before withdrawing his words.
scenes.stakes: Agamemnon's authority and the army's readiness to fight.

scenes.title: Diomed and Sthenelus rebuked
scenes.summary: Agamemnon taunts Diomed with his father Tydeus's courage. Sthenelus retorts and Diomed checks him.
scenes.stakes: Diomed's honour and the cohesion of the Achaean command.

scenes.title: The armies clash
scenes.summary: The silent Achaeans and clamorous Trojans meet, and many warriors fall. Apollo and Minerva urge on their sides.
scenes.stakes: The lives of the warriors on both sides.

Memorable contrast of silent Achaean ranks with noisy Trojans.
Agamemnon's taunt comparing cowering Argives to frightened fawns.

analysis.text: Human war is driven by divine bargaining: Jove yields to Juno, and the truce is broken by Minerva's trick. Fate and divine whim override mortal oaths.
The oaths and sacrifices reflect the Greek belief that oath-breaking invites divine punishment. The Catalogue-style review of captains also shows the honour-based leadership of a warrior aristocracy.

legacy.text: Pandarus's treacherous shot became a standard example of broken faith, and he later appears in Chaucer's and Shakespeare's Troilus stories, though recast as a different figure.

fun_facts.text: The fight over Simoeisius gives a rare detail of Homeric naming, tying his name to the river Simois.

language_notes.text: Nectar is the gods' drink, as ambrosia is their food. Hebe, goddess of youth, serves as cupbearer.
Alexandrus is another name for Paris, the Trojan prince whose abduction of Helen caused the war. Venus rescued him from his duel with Menelaus.
Juno refers to her labour in stirring up the Greeks against Troy, which she wants to see repaid by the city's fall.
"Eat Priam raw" is Jove's exaggeration for Juno's bitter hatred, implying nothing short of total destruction will satisfy her.
"A bone of contention" means a cause of quarrel, like a bone dogs fight over.
"Equitable feasts" means fair, proper shares of sacrifice; the savour of burning fat was the smoke the gods received as their portion.
"She" is Minerva, sent by Jove down from Olympus; the meteor image describes her swift descent, though the name appears in the preceding sentences.
"Requite" means to repay or reward; Alexandrus (Paris) would repay Pandarus for killing his rival Menelaus.
A hecatomb was a large sacrifice, originally of a hundred oxen; here it is vowed as lambs. "Firstling" means first-born of the flock.
"Fool's heart" is the narrator's judgment: Pandarus is foolish to trust the advice, which breaks the truce sworn by both sides.
"Driver of the spoil" is an epithet of Minerva, as goddess who leads war booty; "thee" is the narrator addressing Menelaus.
"Fain" means eager or glad; knights long to carry such a prized cheek-piece, but only a king keeps it.
"Barbs" are the backward-pointing hooks on an arrowhead; if they stayed outside, the wound was shallow.
"Covenant" means the solemn sworn agreement, here the truce and single combat between Menelaus and Paris.
Refers to the sacrifice of lambs, wine offerings and handclasps that sealed the oath before the duel in Book 3.
"He that rules Olympus" is Jove (the Greek Zeus), guardian of oaths, who is expected to punish oath-breakers.
Ilius is Ilium, another name for Troy. The aegis is Jove's storm-shield, shaken to terrify enemies.
"By-word" means an object of scorn, someone people mention as a bad example.
"Wreak his vengeance" is used here sarcastically; the imagined Trojan mocks Agamemnon's failed revenge.
The cuirass is a breastplate. The "belt of mail" is a protective guard worn below it over the abdomen.
Tricca is a town in Thessaly, home of Machaon's contingent.
"Devoured of vultures" means devoured by vultures; "of" is an archaic way of marking the agent.
"Hold his hand over you" is an idiom for shielding or protecting someone.
Heroes were honored with full cups and larger portions at feasts, so a constantly full cup signals special status.
"Facile" here means fluent and smooth; Nestor is the persuasive orator of the Greeks.
"Whether they would or no" means whether they wished to or not; the cowards are forced to fight.
Ereuthalion was an Arcadian champion Nestor killed in his youth, a story he often recalls.
"The other, steeped in cunning" is Ulysses, addressed by his trait rather than his name, an insulting turn.
"Stand you cowering" uses archaic second-person word order; it means "why do you stand cowering." "Brink of battle" means the front edge of the fighting.
Refers to the expedition of the Seven against Thebes: Polynices sought allies to regain his throne from his brother Eteocles.
Achaeans here means the Greeks of Tydeus's party; Cadmeans are the Thebans, named for their founder Cadmus.
"Glibly" means with easy, fluent speech, implying talk without substance.
Sthenelus alludes to the Epigoni, the sons of the Seven, who later captured Thebes after their fathers failed.
"Serried phalanxes" means tightly packed battle lines; "Danaans" is another name for the Greeks, as are Achaeans and Argives.
Panic, Rout and Strife are personified spirits of war. Strife (Eris) is the sister of Mars (the Greek Ares).
The name Simoeisius is tied to the river Simois, where he was born; the poet explains the naming.
A felloe is the curved wooden rim section of a wheel.
Pergamus was the citadel of Troy, where Apollo watches the battle in support of the Trojans.
"The Trito-born" is an epithet of Minerva (the Greek Athena); the meaning of Trito is uncertain.
"Scatheless" means unharmed.

context_notes.text: Juno was patron of Argos, and Minerva was worshipped at Alalcomenae in Boeotia. Both goddesses favour the Greeks.
Argos, Sparta and Mycenae were major Greek cities, the homes of Diomed, Menelaus and Agamemnon. Juno offers them as her price for Troy.
Juno is both Jove's sister and wife, and she cites her rank on both counts.
Pandarus is a Lycian ally of Troy, famed as an archer. Laodocus is a Trojan warrior, so Minerva's disguise wins his trust.
Alexandrus is another name for Paris, who stole Helen from Menelaus. A truce and duel had just been arranged to settle the quarrel.
Apollo was the god of archery, and Pandarus's homeland worshipped him, so the vow suits an archer.
Minerva (the Greek Athena) favours the Achaeans, so she protects Menelaus even while having prompted the shot.
Saturn is the father of Jove, who is therefore called "son of Saturn."
Aesculapius (the Greek Asclepius) was the legendary healer. His sons Machaon and Podalirius serve as physicians to the Achaeans.
Chiron was the wise centaur who taught medicine and healing arts to heroes, including Aesculapius.
Idomeneus leads the Cretan contingent; Meriones is his companion and charioteer-in-arms.
The two Ajaxes are Ajax son of Telamon and Ajax son of Oileus, with their combined troops.
Nestor advises chariot fighters to stay in formation and thrust spears from their chariots, a tactic he claims the ancients used.
Ulysses is identified by his son Telemachus, who is central to the Odyssey.
Diomed, son of Tydeus, is a leading Achaean warrior. Sthenelus is his charioteer and close companion.
Mycenae was Agamemnon's city, so he speaks of its people as "our people."
Tydeus came from Aetolia. His ambush victory shows the heroic courage Agamemnon holds up as a standard.
Democoon is Priam's illegitimate son. Priam is king of Troy.
Achilles withdrew from the fighting after his quarrel with Agamemnon, so the Achaeans lack their greatest warrior.
The Thracians were Trojan allies, known here for the tufts of hair on top of their heads.

literary_notes.text: The narrator openly states Jove's motive, teasing to provoke, so the reader sees his speech as a deliberate test of Juno.
Jove's picture of Juno devouring Priam and all the Trojans exaggerates her hatred with grim, mocking humour.
Juno's seeming indifference to her favourite cities is a bargaining stance. She trades their ruin for Troy's, and the tone is cold.
The swift verb "darted" suggests a falling star or bird, conveying Minerva's eagerness and the sudden start of the coming disaster.
Minerva's rapid, blazing descent is compared to a meteor, an omen sent by Jove, which also hints at the portentous consequences.
The soldiers guess the omen means either war or peace; the reader knows the truce is about to be broken.
The detailed history of the ibex-horn bow shows Pandarus's skill as a hunter and the quality of his weapon.
Minerva's gentle protection is likened to a mother brushing a fly from her sleeping child, a tender domestic image amid violence.
Blood on Menelaus's pale thighs is compared to purple dye on ivory, making the wound beautiful and precious while hinting at his worth.
The vow that Troy will pay with lives, wives and children anticipates the city's eventual fall.
Agamemnon pictures a Trojan's taunt, making the shame of failure vivid and showing how much he fears dishonour.
Agamemnon's wish that the earth swallow him shows the extremity of his grief and shame.
The narrator defends Agamemnon's courage, countering the earlier rebuke and presenting him as a warrior eager for battle.
Agamemnon likens the hesitant soldiers to frightened fawns, shaming them as timid rather than warlike.
Comparing Idomeneus to a wild boar conveys his ferocity before battle.
The extended storm and goat-herd image shows the Ajaxes' dark advancing troops as a looming, unstoppable force.
Agamemnon's quick retraction shows his need to keep the loyalty of proud allies, and Ulysses' touchy pride.
Agamemnon defines Tydeus by courage and leadership, and admits he knows him only by report, which lends the praise a rhetorical edge.
Agamemnon's closing insult contrasts talk with fighting, though Diomed will prove a fierce fighter, so the taunt is unjust.
Diomed's restraint shows discipline and respect for command; he reframes Agamemnon's insult as a leader's duty.
The advancing Greek lines are compared to a wave crashing on rocks, conveying their massed, relentless force.
The disciplined silence of the Greeks is set against the noise of the Trojans in the next sentence.
The Trojan allies' babble is likened to bleating ewes, suggesting disorder and mixed languages.
Strife grows from small to heaven-high, embodying how quarrels swell into war.
Simoeisius falling like a poplar felled for a wheel stresses his youth and the waste of his promise.
The idea of walking unharmed through the carnage under Minerva's guidance emphasizes how dense and deadly the fighting was.
